lead: Semiconductor devices and analog circuits turn a piece of doped silicon into a switch, a voltage reference, an amplifier and a timer. This unit builds that chain step by step: diode, Zener regulator, BJT, FET, op-amp, op-amp circuits, 555 timer. After it you can read a device datasheet, bias a transistor at a Q-point you chose, size a Zener regulator, and find the gain of any standard op-amp circuit from two rules.
about: The unit starts with the physics that makes electronics possible: doped silicon and the PN junction, whose one-way conduction and 0.7 V drop sit under everything that follows. Chapter 4.1 sets out the diode characteristic; 4.2 uses reverse breakdown to build a Zener shunt regulator and moves up to 78xx and LM317 linear regulators. Chapter 4.3 adds the bipolar transistor, a current-controlled device with CE and CB characteristics, and 4.4 the field effect transistor, controlled by gate voltage instead. Chapter 4.5 treats the op-amp as a very high gain differential amplifier and derives the two golden rules; 4.6 applies those rules to the follower, adder, subtractor, integrator and comparator. Chapter 4.7, tagged advanced, covers the 555 timer built from comparators and a flip-flop.

chapters.idea: Doping makes p-type and n-type silicon, and the junction between them conducts easily in one direction above about 0.7 V, which is the whole diode.
chapters.depth: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, trivalent and pentavalent doping, majority and minority carriers. The junction at equilibrium: depletion region, barrier potential 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. Forward and reverse bias, knee voltage, reverse saturation current (nA for silicon, µA for germanium), breakdown. The static V-I characteristic, also called the diode characteristic; ideal versus practical diode. One short section on the diode applications the syllabi list: half-wave and full-wave rectifier (ripple factor 1.21 and 0.482, efficiency 40.6% and 81.2%) and clippers.

figure.aria: Plot of silicon diode current against voltage: nearly zero until about 0.6 V forward, then a steep rise, with the reverse side flat at almost zero current.

chapters.example: A silicon diode in series with a 220 Ω resistor is connected to the 5 V output of a phone charger. The diode drop is 0.7 V. Find the diode current and the power it dissipates. Answer: I = (5 − 0.7)/220 = 19.5 mA; P = 0.7 V × 19.5 mA = 13.7 mW.
chapters.trap: Using the ideal diode with a 0 V drop when the 0.7 V silicon drop decides the current, and drawing the arrow backwards: the triangle points from anode (p side) to cathode (n side).
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Ohm's law, KVL and series circuits.
chapters.leave: Rectifier filter-capacitor design and ripple derivations, small-signal ac resistance of the diode, and LEDs and photodiodes.

chapters.idea: A reverse-biased Zener holds almost the same voltage across itself even when its current changes, so it can hold a load voltage steady.
chapters.depth: Zener action in reverse breakdown: heavy doping, a thin depletion layer, Zener breakdown below about 5 V and avalanche breakdown above it. Ratings: Vz, Iz(min), Iz(max), dynamic resistance Zz, power Pz = Vz × Iz. Shunt regulator design with the series resistor Rs = (Vin − Vz)/(Iz + IL), and line and load regulation as a percentage. Then three-terminal fixed regulators (78xx positive, 79xx negative) and the adjustable LM317 with Vout = 1.25(1 + R2/R1); dropout voltage and ripple rejection. Some syllabi call the device a breakdown diode or a reference diode.

figure.aria: Block diagram: unregulated 12 V passes through series resistor Rs to the output node, where a reverse-biased 6 V Zener and the load sit in parallel.

chapters.example: A 6 V Zener must feed a load current varying from 20 mA to 50 mA from an unregulated 12 V supply that can sag to 10 V. Take Iz(min) = 5 mA and Iz(max) = 100 mA. Choose Rs and the Zener power rating. Answer: Rs(max) = (10 − 6)/(5 mA + 50 mA) = 72.7 Ω; Rs(min) = (12 − 6)/(100 mA + 20 mA) = 50 Ω; choose the standard 68 Ω. At 10 V supply with full load, Iz = 4/68 − 50 mA = 8.8 mA, still above 5 mA. At 12 V with light load, Iz = 6/68 − 20 mA = 68.2 mA, so Pz = 6 V × 68.2 mA = 0.41 W; fit a 1 W Zener.
chapters.trap: Sizing Rs from the no-load case only, so the Zener burns out at full load; and assuming regulation continues when Vin < Vz or when Iz falls below Iz(min), where the output simply follows the input.
chapters.prereq: 4.1: reverse characteristics and breakdown of the PN junction.
chapters.leave: Transistor series regulators and error amplifiers (4.3), switching regulators and SMPS, battery charging circuits.

chapters.idea: In a BJT a small base current controls a much larger collector current, so the device behaves as a current-controlled current source.
chapters.depth: NPN and PNP construction: emitter heavily doped, base thin and lightly doped, collector large in area. Forward-biased base-emitter junction and reverse-biased collector-base junction. Current relations IE = IB + IC, α = IC/IE (0.95 to 0.99), β = IC/IB (50 to 300), β = α/(1 − α). Cut-off, active and saturation regions. Biasing methods: fixed base, collector-to-base feedback, voltage divider and emitter bias; dc load line and Q-point. Input and output characteristics of the CE (NPN) and CB (NPN) configurations and what each region of the output curve means. Also called a bipolar transistor or simply a transistor.

figure.aria: Plot of CE output characteristics for an NPN transistor: each base current gives a curve that rises steeply near zero VCE and then stays almost flat as VCE increases.

chapters.example: A fixed-base NPN circuit has VCC = 12 V, RB = 470 kΩ, RC = 2.2 kΩ, β = 100 and VBE = 0.7 V. Find IB, IC and VCE, and state the region. Answer: IB = (12 − 0.7)/470 kΩ = 24.0 µA; IC = 100 × 24.0 µA = 2.40 mA; VCE = 12 − 2.40 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 6.7 V. Since VCE is well above 0.2 V the transistor is in the active region (IC(sat) would be 12/2.2 kΩ = 5.45 mA).
chapters.trap: Assuming the active region without checking: IC = βIB holds only while VCE stays above about 0.2 V; otherwise the device is saturated and IC = (VCC − 0.2)/RC, whatever β says.
chapters.prereq: 4.1, because the base-emitter junction is a diode, and Unit 1 for KVL and load lines.
chapters.leave: Small-signal h-parameter models, amplifier gain and frequency response, biasing stability calculations, and the FET in 4.4.

chapters.idea: In a FET the gate voltage sets the width of a conducting channel, so drain current is controlled by voltage and the gate draws almost no current.
chapters.depth: JFET: n-channel construction, gate-channel junction always reverse biased, VGS(off) (also called pinch-off voltage VP) and IDSS. Transfer characteristic ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))² and the drain characteristics with ohmic and saturation regions. MOSFET: depletion and enhancement types; n-channel enhancement MOSFET with metal gate, thin oxide and threshold VT; inversion layer and ID = k(VGS − VT)² in saturation. Symbols, very high input resistance (order of 10¹⁰ Ω), and a short BJT-versus-FET comparison. Also called a unipolar transistor, IGFET or MOS device.

figure.aria: Plot of the JFET transfer characteristic for IDSS = 8 mA and VGS(off) = −4 V: drain current is zero at −4 V and rises as a square law to 8 mA at 0 V.

chapters.example: An n-channel JFET has IDSS = 8 mA and VGS(off) = −4 V. It is biased at VGS = −2 V with RD = 2.2 kΩ and VDD = 15 V. Find ID, VDS and the transconductance gm. Answer: ID = 8(1 − (−2)/(−4))² = 8 × 0.25 = 2 mA; VDS = VDD − ID × RD = 15 − 2 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 10.6 V; gm0 = 2IDSS/|VGS(off)| = 4 mS, so gm = 4(1 − 0.5) mS = 2 mS.
chapters.trap: Sign errors in VGS(off) (negative for an n-channel JFET) and using the square law outside saturation; also expecting gate current in a MOSFET, where the oxide layer insulates the gate.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the reverse-biased junction and depletion region, and 4.3 for the comparison.
chapters.leave: MOSFET switching and gate-drive circuits, CMOS logic gates (Unit 5) and FET amplifier design.

chapters.idea: An op-amp multiplies the difference between its two inputs by a very large gain, and negative feedback turns that unwieldy gain into a precise one set by two resistors.
chapters.depth: Symbol, supply pins and the eight pins of the LM741 (offset null 1 and 5, inverting input 2, non-inverting input 3, V− 4, output 6, V+ 7). Typical 741 values: open-loop gain 2 × 10⁵, input resistance 2 MΩ, output resistance 75 Ω, unity-gain bandwidth 1 MHz, slew rate 0.5 V/µs. Ideal op-amp assumptions, output saturation near ±(VCC − 1 V), and the equivalent circuit: input resistance, dependent source A × Vd, output resistance. Open-loop configuration, then closed-loop inverting gain −Rf/Rin and non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R1, with the virtual short and virtual ground rules. Also called an opamp or a linear IC.

figure.aria: Block diagram of an op-amp: the two inputs feed a difference stage, which drives a very high gain stage whose output saturates at the supply rails.

chapters.example: An inverting amplifier uses R1 = 10 kΩ and Rf = 100 kΩ with supplies of ±12 V. The input is 0.5 V. Find the closed-loop gain, the output voltage and the current in R1. Answer: gain = −Rf/R1 = −10; Vout = −10 × 0.5 V = −5 V, inside the ±12 V rails so there is no clipping; current in R1 = 0.5 V/10 kΩ = 50 µA, and the same 50 µA flows in Rf.
chapters.trap: Applying the virtual short rule without negative feedback: an open-loop or positive-feedback op-amp sits at saturation, so V+ = V− is no longer true.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for KCL, Ohm's law and the potential divider; 4.3 for the transistor stages inside the chip.
chapters.leave: Transistor-level analysis and compensation of the 741, offset and drift calculations, active filters, and the applications collected in 4.6.

chapters.idea: One op-amp plus a few resistors or one capacitor gives addition, subtraction, integration and comparison, all from the same two golden rules.
chapters.depth: Voltage follower (gain 1, very high input resistance, used as a buffer between a sensor and a load). Inverting adder Vout = −Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2 + V3/R3) and averaging with equal resistors; non-inverting adder in one line. Difference amplifier, balanced when Rf/R1 = R3/R2, giving Vout = (Rf/R1)(V2 − V1). Integrator Vout = −(1/R1C)∫Vin dt, square wave to triangle and sine to cosine; differentiator as the mirror circuit. Comparator with a reference, zero-crossing detector, and the Schmitt trigger in one line.

figure.aria: Plot of an integrator fed with a ±1 V square wave of 1 ms half period: the output is a triangle wave falling while the input is high and rising while it is low.

chapters.example: An inverting adder has Rf = 20 kΩ and three input resistors of 10 kΩ each, fed with V1 = 1 V, V2 = 2 V and V3 = 0.5 V. Supplies are ±12 V. Find Vout and the current through Rf. Answer: Vout = −(20/10)(1 + 2 + 0.5) = −7 V, inside the rails; current through Rf = 7 V/20 kΩ = 0.35 mA.
chapters.trap: Treating the comparator as a linear amplifier and expecting an output proportional to the input difference; with no feedback the output is only ever near +Vsat or −Vsat.
chapters.prereq: 4.5, especially the virtual short rule and the saturation limits.
chapters.leave: Precision rectifiers, instrumentation amplifiers, active filter design and the differentiator's noise problems.

chapters.idea: A 555 timer compares a rising capacitor voltage with two fixed levels and flips its output, so one resistor and one capacitor set the timing.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this, so keep it short. Internal blocks: three equal resistors setting ⅓ VCC and ⅔ VCC, two comparators, an RS flip-flop, a discharge transistor and an output stage. Monostable time T = 1.1RC. Astable period T = 0.693(R1 + 2R2)C, frequency f = 1.44/((R1 + 2R2)C), duty cycle = (R1 + R2)/(R1 + 2R2). Applications: LED blinker, time delay, tone generator, PWM and switch debouncing.

figure.aria: Block diagram of the 555 timer: a trigger below one third of the supply sets the flip-flop and drives the output high, while a threshold above two thirds resets it and turns on the discharge transistor.

chapters.example: A 555 astable uses R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 47 kΩ and C = 10 µF. Find the period, the frequency and the duty cycle. Answer: R1 + 2R2 = 104 kΩ; T = 0.693 × 104 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ s = 0.72 s; f = 1.44/(104 × 10³ × 10 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.38 Hz; duty cycle = (10 + 47)/104 = 54.8%.
chapters.trap: Unit slips — C must be in farads and R in ohms — and expecting a duty cycle below 50%: this circuit charges through R1 + R2 but discharges through R2 only, so the high time is always longer.
chapters.prereq: 4.6 for the comparator idea and Unit 1 for RC charging with time constant τ = RC.
chapters.leave: Precision timers, VCO and PLL circuits, and microcontroller timers, which belong to Unit 5.
